title: If…: the conditional -sa and the word deb
goal: Build conditional sentences, and quote what others say with *deb* — the little word that covers every "that" in Uzbek.
bekal: quoting and giving opinions with *… deb aytdi* and *… deb oʻylayman*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Havo yaxshi boʻlsa, chiqamiz
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon. Weekend plans are being made in the group chat, but the forecast is uncertain.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.id: Shall we go up the mountain tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: If the weather's good, we'll go.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Unda uyda qolamiz. Men film koʻramiz deb oʻylayman.
lines.id: Then we'll stay home. I think we'll watch a movie.
lines.literal: that-in home-at stay-we. I film watch-we saying think-I.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.id: Our teacher said "the mountain road is closed".

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rostdanmi? Unda boshqa joyga borsak boʻladi.
lines.id: Really? Then we can go somewhere else.
lines.literal: truly-? that-in other place-to go-if-we becomes.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Chorvoqqa borsak-chi? U yerda koʻl bor.
lines.id: How about Chorvoq? There's a lake there.
lines.literal: Chorvoq-to go-if-we-and? that place-in lake exists.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.text: Zoʻr fikr! Agar erta tursak, tushga yetib boramiz.
lines.id: Great idea! If we get up early, we'll be there by noon.
lines.literal: great thought! if early rise-if-we, noon-to reaching go-we.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Soat oltida chiqsak boʻladimi? Men erta turaman.
lines.id: Can we leave at six? I get up early anyway.
lines.literal: hour six-at leave-if-we becomes-? I early rise-I.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: OK. If you're late, we won't wait!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I promise I won't be late!

notes: **Agar can be dropped.** *Agar havo yaxshi boʻlsa* and *Havo yaxshi boʻlsa* are both correct — the ending *-sa* already carries the meaning "if". *Agar* just reinforces it.
**Deb literally means "saying".** It goes **after** the quote, not before: *"Togʻ yoʻli yopiq" deb aytdi*. English puts "that" in front; Uzbek puts *deb* at the end.
**-sa-chi? means "what about…?"** The conditional combined with the *-chi* ending from unit 12. *Borsak-chi?* = "how about we go?" — the gentlest way to suggest something.
**Rostdanmi? = "really?"** From *rost* (true, real). Its cousins: *chinmi?* and *haqiqatanmi?*. All three express surprise.

grammars.title: -sa: the conditional form
body: The formula: stem + *-sa* + person ending. The person endings are the same set as the past *-di* form, except for the first person singular.
after: **The negative inserts -ma- as usual**: *bormasam* (if I don't go), *kechikmasangiz* (if you're not late).
For noun sentences, use *boʻlsa*: *Havo yaxshi boʻlsa* (if the weather's good), *Vaqtingiz boʻlsa* (if you have time), *Kerak boʻlsa* (if necessary). Three expressions you'll use constantly.
The "if" clause always comes **before** the main clause: *Yomgʻir yogʻsa, uyda qolamiz*. Reversing it isn't wrong, but it sounds like an afterthought.

grammars.title: Deb: one word for "that", "said", and "so as to"
body: *Deb* is the *-ib* form of *demoq* (to say). It comes after whatever is quoted, thought, or given as a reason.

head: Use
Example
Meaning
rows: She promised she wouldn't be late.

after: ⚠️ **The quote keeps its original form.** Unlike English, Uzbek doesn't shift the pronouns: *"Men kelaman" deb aytdi* = literally "he said 'I'll come'", and that's the correct way to say "he said he'd come".
*Deb oʻylayman* (I think) and *deb hisoblayman* (I consider) are the two most common ways to give an opinion. A more casual cousin: *menimcha* from unit 16.
The question word is *nima deb* — "what (did they say)", "what is it called": *Bu oʻzbekcha nima deb ataladi?* = "what's this called in Uzbek?". The most useful sentence for any language learner.

blocks.text: Ten ready-made forms. They all use *-sa*, and they all come up many times a day.

*Xudo xohlasa* literally means "if God wills" — the exact equivalent of *inshallah*, and used just as often. The Arabic form *inshaAlloh* is used too. It can be a sincere promise or a polite refusal; the tone decides which.
Uzbekistan borders no sea at all — it's one of only two countries in the world whose neighbors are landlocked too. What it has instead are mountains, reservoirs, and deserts.

⚠️ *Daryo* means **river**, not sea — even though Persian "darya" means sea, and the names of Central Asia's two great rivers, *Amudaryo* (Amu Darya) and *Sirdaryo* (Syr Darya), use that word. *Osmon* (sky) is also from Persian, while *dengiz* is a native Turkic word.

Chorvoq is a reservoir at the foot of the Tian Shan mountains, about an hour and a half from Tashkent — the most popular weekend getaway. A useful sentence: *Chorvoqqa qanday boriladi?* (how do you get to Chorvoq?).

vocab.en: to go up; to go out

exercises.prompt: Put into the conditional (-sa) for the given subject.

items: If the weather's good, we'll go up the mountain.
If it rains, we'll stay home.
If you have time, call me.
How about we go to the lake?

exercises.prompt: Join the two sentences with the conditional. Example: Havo yaxshi. Chiqamiz. → Havo yaxshi boʻlsa, chiqamiz.
Put the words in the right order.
Spaced review — unit 17. Translate into Uzbek without looking back at the unit.
